sceneEn: You are talking to a friend about your plans for the year: what you intend to learn, which habit you want to build, what you will give up. Describe your plans with the zu infinitive.
partnerEn: a friend who takes your plans seriously and asks questions
openingEn: You said this year was going to be different. So what have you set yourself?
goalEn: What you intend to learn, which habit you will build and what you will give up have all been described.

sceneEn: You are having a goals meeting with a course adviser: what you want to achieve in what time, what your intermediate steps are, how you will measure progress.
partnerEn: a course adviser who wants concrete numbers
openingEn: Before we pick a course: what exactly do you want to achieve in the next six months?
goalEn: The timescale, the goal and the intermediate steps have been made clear, and it has been settled how progress will be measured.

sceneEn: You are at the office of a language school: compare the intensive course with the evening course, ask about the price, the pace and the group size, then choose one with your reasons.
partnerEn: an honest course secretary who knows both courses well
openingEn: We have two courses that would suit you. What would you like to decide on?
goalEn: The two courses have been compared and one has been chosen with reasons.

sceneEn: You are talking to your teacher before the exam: say what you are apprehensive about, which part you find hard and what you will do if it happens. Build your sentences with conditional clauses.
partnerEn: a teacher who calms you down and gives concrete advice
openingEn: You seem tense. What do you have most respect for in the exam?
goalEn: The part you are apprehensive about has been named, what you will do if it happens has been discussed and a strategy has been agreed.

sceneEn: You are discussing a request for training with your boss: say why you want it in clauses of purpose, say what the company gains, and discuss the funding and the working arrangements.
partnerEn: a boss who thinks about the budget but keeps an open mind
openingEn: You wanted to talk about some training. What exactly do you need it for?
goalEn: The aim of the training, what the company gains and the funding have been discussed, and your boss has given an answer.

sceneEn: You are at the university's student advice service: ask about the application deadline, the documents needed and which course would suit you. Put your questions indirectly.
partnerEn: a practical student adviser who has talked to a great many students
openingEn: Do sit down. You're interested in studying with us — what would you like to clear up first?
goalEn: The application deadline, the documents needed and the course that suits you have all been found out.

sceneEn: At a job interview you are describing your internship: which company, how long it lasted, what work you did, what you got out of it. Tell it in the past tense of written German.
partnerEn: an HR specialist taking notes and asking for detail
openingEn: There's an internship on your CV. Do tell us briefly: what did you do there?
goalEn: Where the internship was, how long it lasted, the work you did and what you got out of it have all been described.

sceneEn: You and a fellow student are comparing how you learn: what you study and how, what works, what does not. Say two things at once with paired conjunctions.
partnerEn: a curious fellow student who defends their own method
openingEn: Tell me, how do you actually learn? My method isn't getting me anywhere at the moment.
goalEn: Your two methods have been compared and you have decided to try something from each other.

sceneEn: You are talking to a friend about the fear of making mistakes: why you hold back when you speak, what you carry on in spite of, how you take your mistakes. Build clauses of contrast.
partnerEn: a reassuring friend who talks about their own mistakes freely
openingEn: You hardly say a thing in class, even though you know a lot. What's holding you back?
goalEn: The reason for holding back has been described and what you will carry on in spite of has been said.

sceneEn: You are discussing a career decision with your mentor: describe your options, ask what they would do, ask for feedback. Build the exchange of advice in the subjunctive.
partnerEn: an experienced mentor who speaks directly
openingEn: So you're facing a decision. Tell me what options you can see — what would you most like to do?
goalEn: The options have been described, your mentor's view has been heard and a next step has been settled.

sceneEn: You are discussing a new decision in the city with an acquaintance: restricting cars in the centre. Give your opinion, justify it, and separate the points you agree with from the ones you do not.
partnerEn: an acquaintance who defends their own view and enjoys an argument
openingEn: Have you heard? Cars are going to be banned from the city centre soon. What do you make of that?
goalEn: Your opinion has been given with reasons and the points you agree and disagree with have been separated.

sceneEn: A friend is thinking of moving out of the city and is asking what you think. Set the pros and cons side by side with paired conjunctions, and say at the end which weighs more.
partnerEn: an undecided friend who wants to hear both sides
openingEn: We're thinking of moving to the country. Be honest: what's for it and what's against it?
goalEn: The pros and cons have been weighed up and it has been said which weighs more.

sceneEn: In a meeting you disagree with a colleague's proposal. First show that you have understood them, then put your reservation in soft forms, and suggest a compromise at the end.
partnerEn: a reasonable colleague who is attached to their proposal
openingEn: I suggest we put the project back by three months. How do you see it?
goalEn: The other side has been shown to be understood, the reservation has been put and a compromise has been suggested.

sceneEn: At a parents' evening you are discussing children's screen time: how much you think is right, what it depends on, how it should be limited. Build your opinion with fixed-preposition verbs.
partnerEn: an anxious parent who wants firm rules
openingEn: Two hours a day — that's far too much for a child. Do you see it that way too?
goalEn: How much is right, what it depends on and how it should be limited have all been discussed.

sceneEn: An acquaintance is telling you a surprising piece of news. Question the claim: find out where it came from, who said it and whether it has been confirmed, with indirect questions.
partnerEn: an excitable acquaintance who believes what they hear straight away
openingEn: Have you read this? From next year it's supposedly going to be banned completely. Did you know that?
goalEn: The source of the claim has been questioned and it has been made clear whether it has been confirmed.

sceneEn: You and a friend are arguing about the finale of the series you watched: what you liked, what you liked it in spite of, what ending you would have expected. Build clauses of contrast and expectation.
partnerEn: a friend who loved the finale and is trying to win you over
openingEn: Well I thought the finale was superb. But you pulled such a face — what didn't you like?
goalEn: What you liked and disliked about the finale has been said and the ending you expected has been described.

sceneEn: At the book club you are discussing the book you read: which part moved you, where it was heavy going, who you would recommend it to. Describe the book with relative clauses.
partnerEn: a club member who gave up halfway and wants to be persuaded
openingEn: I got stuck on page eighty. Is it really worth reading on?
goalEn: The moving and the heavy parts of the book have been described and it has been said who it is for.

sceneEn: You and a friend are arguing about your taste in music: which is better, why, what matters more to you. Compare, and close the argument politely.
partnerEn: a jokey friend who defends their own music
openingEn: How can you listen to that? It's the same rhythm all the way through. What do you see in it?
goalEn: Your tastes have been compared and the argument has been closed politely.

sceneEn: You have come out of an exhibition and you are telling a friend about it: which work stayed with you, what it reminded you of, how it made you feel. Build it with fixed-preposition verbs.
partnerEn: a curious friend who does not know much about art
openingEn: So, how was the exhibition? I don't understand much about art — what stayed with you?
goalEn: The work that stayed with you, what it called to mind and how it made you feel have all been described.

sceneEn: You are in a short debate: the subject is shops opening at the weekend. Give your view, line up your reasons and close your turn with a summary.
partnerEn: a debating opponent who argues the other side and keeps the time
openingEn: Two minutes each. I'll start: shops should stay shut on Sundays. What do you say to that?
goalEn: Your view has been given, at least two reasons have been lined up and the turn has been closed with a summary.

sceneEn: You are at the GP's describing a complaint that has gone on for months: since when, when it gets worse, what it might be connected with. Describe it with fixed-preposition verbs.
partnerEn: a GP who takes their time and asks for detail
openingEn: Do sit down. You said on the phone it's been going on a while — since when exactly?
goalEn: How long the complaint has lasted and what it might be connected with have been described, and the doctor has said the next step.

sceneEn: You are ringing a specialist's practice: say you have a referral, ask for an appointment, and ask about the waiting time and what you need to bring.
partnerEn: a receptionist with a full appointment book who talks fast on the phone
openingEn: Dr Ahrens' practice, good afternoon. Do you have a referral from your GP?
goalEn: An appointment has been made and the waiting time and what to bring have been found out.

sceneEn: You are asking for advice at the pharmacy: say which medicines you are already taking, ask whether the new one can be taken with them, ask about the dose and the timing. Put your questions in conditional clauses.
partnerEn: a careful pharmacist who checks the leaflet
openingEn: Good afternoon. Before I give you this: are you taking any other medicines at the moment?
goalEn: The medicines you take have been given, the interaction has been asked about and the dose and timing have been made clear.

sceneEn: You are talking to a nutritionist: how you eat, what you are trying to change, what you find hard. Build your sentences with infinitive phrases.
partnerEn: a nutritionist who does not judge and gives concrete suggestions
openingEn: Just tell me about an ordinary day: what do you eat in the morning, at midday, in the evening?
goalEn: How you eat has been described, along with what you are trying to change and what you find hard.

sceneEn: You are discussing your back pain with a physiotherapist: when it starts, how you sit during the day, what they recommend. Discuss the advice in the subjunctive.
partnerEn: a physiotherapist who gives practical advice and gets you moving
openingEn: Show me how you sit at your desk. When does it hurt most?
goalEn: When the pain started and how you sit have been described, and a concrete suggestion has been taken away.
